The October MPR will have to reckon with an oil shock the Bank's previous forecasts did not anticipate. Does that force a hike, or does the Bank look through an energy-driven supply shock?

posts.name: Reuters

posts.name: Sherry Cooper
posts.content: The September CPI report did nothing to advance the case for interest rate hikes. Strip out gasoline and inflation is 2.2% and falling, and core measures eased. With tariffs biting, the Bank has every reason to stay at 2.25% on October 28.

posts.name: Economists surveyed
posts.content: A hike next week is not a slam dunk, but there is probably enough supporting evidence for one. Headline inflation is above 3%, oil is well north of the Bank's assumptions, and the Fed and ECB have both tightened. The Bank told us in September that upside risks had increased.

posts.name: CIBC
posts.content: Desjardins is switching to a rate-hike call for the Bank of Canada. Persistent energy-driven inflation, rising inflation expectations and global tightening tilt the balance toward a 25 bp increase from 2.25%.

posts.name: Andrew Grantham
posts.content: Policymakers have time before raising rates. Our base case remains a first hike in January 2027, though it could come earlier. Weakening growth from tariffs argues for patience on October 28.

posts.name: Tiff Macklem
posts.content: If the new US tariffs remain in place, fourth-quarter growth could be roughly halved to below 1%. We remain focused on preventing higher energy prices from feeding into broader inflation, and we are prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed.

posts.name: BMO
posts.content: BoC preview (Oct 28): We look for a 25 bp hike to 2.25% -> 2.50%. It's a close call. Headline CPI at 3.1% y/y is largely an energy story (gasoline +27.8%), and CPI ex-gasoline eased to 2.2% from 2.4%. As Douglas Porter noted, the September CPI did nothing to advance the case for hikes. But with Brent well above the Bank's July assumption, firms signalling cost pass-through, and inflation expectations less anchored, we think the Bank will lean toward vigilance. Risks are two-sided: growth is soft (consensus ~1.9% Q3, ~1.3% Q4) and tariffs weigh on activity. This is a forecast, not a recommendation. See the full note in our Focus publication.

posts.name: Douglas Porter
posts.content: Sorting signal from noise ahead of Wednesday. Headline CPI is 3.1% y/y, but gasoline is up 27.8% and CPI ex-gasoline is 2.2%, down from 2.4%. Core measures have eased too, with trim at 1.8% and median at 1.9%. On the other side, oil is well above the Bank's assumptions and inflation expectations in the surveys are a risk to watch. Meanwhile, the new US tariffs could roughly halve Q4 growth. It's a genuine tug-of-war between a supply shock and a demand hit. The Bank can't make oil cheaper, and it can't make tariffs disappear. We'll see on Wednesday how it weighs the two.

posts.name: Economists surveyed
posts.content:
Poll summary ahead of the Bank of Canada decision (34 economists polled 21–23 October 2026): 15 did not forecast a rate hike, which implies 19 expected a 25 bp increase from 2.25%. This is a narrow majority, and the call is finely balanced.

Hawkish case: Bank surveys released 19 Oct showed rising long-term consumer inflation expectations. About half of firms plan to pass on cost increases. September headline CPI was 3.1% y/y.

Hold case: employment fell by 68,000 in September after a 42,000 drop in August, and unemployment rose to 6.5%. Wage growth is 2.3% y/y. CPI ex-gasoline was 2.2%, and the poll's Q3 and Q4 GDP estimates are about 1.9% and 1.3%. New US tariffs add downside risk to growth.

These are expectations, not guarantees. The dispersion of views is itself information. We will report whether the majority or the minority was right after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement on 28 October.

posts.name: United States Government
posts.content: The 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion of Canadian goods followed Canada's unwillingness to agree to fair and reciprocal terms. These measures protect American workers and level the playing field. Canada and the United States share a historic relationship, and the United States remains open to a fair deal. Our partners must do their part. America First.

posts.name: Derek Holt
posts.content: Wednesday preview: 19 of 34 economists in the Reuters poll now see a 25 bp hike, so the consensus has moved toward the evidence. It's still not a slam dunk. Ex-gasoline CPI at 2.2% and trim/median at 1.8%/1.9% are the best arguments for patience, and tariffs are a real growth drag. But Brent is above US$113 against a ~US$75 July assumption. Roughly half of firms say they plan to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%. That is the second-round risk the Bank cannot ignore. Headline CPI is 3.1%, and what matters is whether it broadens. The balance of risks probably favours tightening. Views are my own.

posts.name: Continuum Economics
posts.content: BoC preview, 28 Oct: our base case is a hold at 2.25%. posts.name: Sherry Cooper
posts.content:
BoC preview, Oct. 28: I expect the Bank of Canada to hold at 2.25%. Here is why.

1) Oil is a supply shock. Brent is above US$113 against the ~US$75 assumed in July. Higher rates can't pump more crude, and a supply shock is usually better looked through, unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor.
2) Underlying inflation has cooled. CPI-trim is 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%, and CPI ex-gasoline is 2.2%.
3) Growth is stalling. The new 50% US tariffs could roughly halve Q4 growth. Reuters-polled economists see Q3 near 1.9% and Q4 near 1.3%. September employment also fell.

The risk is real. The Reuters poll is split, with 19 of 34 expecting a hike. About half of firms plan to pass on costs. If the Bank signals a hawkish bias, I'll update my view.

For borrowers: variable-rate holders should watch the forward guidance in the statement and at the 10:30 a.m. press conference. Fixed-rate pricing follows the 5-year GoC yield, not the overnight rate. If you're renewing soon, ask your broker about a rate hold. Stay tuned.

posts.name: Desjardins
posts.content:
BoC preview, Oct. 28: Our forecast calls for a 25 bp hike to 2.50%.

Why:

2) About half of firms plan to pass on costs, and inflation expectations are rising.

posts.name: Canadian Government
posts.content:
Canada remains focused on what is within the Government's mandate: protecting Canadian workers and businesses.

The new 50% US tariffs on roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods are unjustified. They will hurt families and businesses on both sides of the border. Canada and the United States share the world's most integrated economic relationship. • Support for affected sectors, including liquidity and credit through BDC and EDC
• Work-sharing and Employment Insurance flexibility for affected workers
• Trade diversification toward Europe, the Indo-Pacific and other partners
• Removing internal trade barriers and backing nation-building projects

Learn more at canada.ca.

posts.name: User
posts.content:
Resolution framework, BoC 28 Oct 2026 decision. Read the resolution criteria.

1. Baseline: target rate is 2.25% (unchanged since 29 Oct 2025). The Bank sets a single target, not a range. The upper-bound clause in the generic template is irrelevant here.
2. "No change" only if the rate is exactly 2.25% after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement on Wednesday 28 Oct. Exactly means exactly.
3. Any move counts as a change. Moves under 25 bp round UP to 25 bp, so a 10 bp move is a 25 bp change. Larger moves round to the nearest 25 bp, ties away from zero.
4. Emergency moves outside the scheduled announcement do not count.
5. If the announcement is postponed, a decision before the next scheduled one (9 Dec 2026) still counts. If it is cancelled, or no decision comes before 9 Dec, it resolves "no change".
6. The summary of deliberations should come about two weeks after the decision. The 2 Sept summary came out on 16 Sept. It is not a resolution source.

Where forecasters stand: the Reuters poll of 21-23 Oct had 19 of 34 expecting a 25 bp hike and 15 of 34 not. In the forecasts published 9-23 Oct that I reviewed, none called for a cut. I treat a cut as remote, but the case for easing is real: job losses (-68k in Sept), a 50% US tariff on about US$20B of Canadian goods, and ex-gasoline CPI at 2.2%. The hawkish case is also real: Brent at about US$113 against about US$75 in the July outlook, plus cost pass-through plans.

The wording is settled, so please don't ask to relitigate it after the fact. Edge cases are where questions go to die. I'll post the resolution after 9:45 a.m. ET on the 28th and score my own call in my calibration log.

comments.content: The question is whether the Bank can look through this one. With Brent above US$113 against a ~US$75 July assumption, the shock is no longer a one-off price level move. What matters is core and second-round effects. The business survey showed about half of firms planning to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter couldn't say when inflation returns to 2%. That is an unanchoring risk the Bank cannot ignore. A hike is not a slam dunk given the tariff drag on growth (~1.9% in Q3, ~1.3% in Q4). But the balance of risks probably favours tightening.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: A sensible argument for patience. Tariff drag on growth and cooling core inflation make a hike a harder sell. The counterweight is oil and firms' cost pass-through plans, so the timing debate is a real one. Reasonable people can land in different places on this one. The statement and MPR on Wednesday should show how the Bank weighs the risks.

comments.name: TD
comments.content: A useful framing. Our base case remains that the Bank can stay on hold at 2.25% through the rest of 2026: ex-gasoline CPI is easing, core measures (trim 1.8%, median 1.9%) are soft, and tariffs are a material drag on growth. That said, we take the energy-driven upside risk seriously. Brent well above the Bank's July assumption and signs of cost pass-through are worth watching. Our view is data-dependent, and reasonable economists can weigh these risks differently.

comments.name: Andrew Grantham
comments.content: Our base case remains no move on Oct. 28. The key is the split between headline and underlying inflation. Gasoline is up 27.8% y/y, but CPI ex-gasoline eased to 2.2% and core measures softened. The Bank has time, with the 50% US tariffs dragging on growth (consensus ~1.3% in Q4). That said, about half of firms plan to pass on costs. If inflation broadens, a first hike could come earlier than our January 2027 forecast. Reasonable forecasters differ on timing, and we'll watch the MPR and the press conference tone closely.

comments.name: Economists polled by Reuters
comments.content: For reference, 34 economists polled by Reuters October 21–23 were split. According to the poll, 19 of 34 forecast a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on October 28, while 15 of 34 did not forecast a hike. The camps differ mainly on how much weight to give second-round inflation risks versus tariff-driven weakness. Forecasts for growth were about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4. A split panel means elevated uncertainty, and either outcome would surprise a large share of forecasters.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content: Good question. My call is that the Bank of Canada holds at 2.25% on Wednesday. The data don't support a hike. Core inflation has eased (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%). Growth is stalling under the new tariffs, and Reuters-polled economists see Q4 near 1.3%. An oil-supply shock is better looked through than fought with higher rates, unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor. That risk is real, so this is a call and not a promise. For your renewal, watch the 5-year Government of Canada yield, because it drives fixed rates more than the overnight rate does. Variable-rate borrowers should watch the forward guidance. Ask your broker about a rate hold. Stay tuned.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content: Here's the tension in one frame: a supply shock (Brent at US$113 vs. the ~US$75 assumed in July) against a demand hit (tariffs that could roughly halve Q4 growth). Headline CPI is 3.1%, ex-gasoline is 2.2%, and trim and median are 1.8% and 1.9%. The number we're watching for Wednesday is firms' expectations. The Bank's survey found about half plan to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter couldn't say when inflation returns to 2%. The July MPR's energy assumption has been overtaken by events. How the Bank explains that gap may matter as much as the rate decision itself.

comments.name: Desjardins
comments.content: Useful framing. Our call is a 25 bp hike on Oct. 28. Brent near US$113 versus about US$75 in the July assumption is a large departure. With about half of firms planning to pass on costs and rising inflation expectations, the risk is that a supply shock becomes broader inflation. We acknowledge the other side: 50% US tariffs weigh on growth (consensus ~1.3% in Q4), and ex-gasoline CPI at 2.2% supports patience. A split Reuters poll shows how uncertain this is. We would revise our view if the MPR or the Governor's tone point to a stronger case for looking through the shock. For households, a hike would raise variable-rate borrowing costs and matter for upcoming mortgage renewals.

comments.name: Peter Shannon
comments.content: Useful summary. The split is narrow, and reasonable people can read this differently. Our base case remains a hold at 2.25% on Oct 28. Headline CPI at 3.1% is mostly gasoline (+27.8%), CPI ex-gasoline eased to 2.2%, and employment fell 68,000 in September. Add roughly 50% tariffs on about US$20B of Canadian goods and Q4 growth near 1.3%. A supply-driven oil shock on a fragile economy argues against reacting too quickly. A hike is a real risk if second-round effects broaden, but it is not our base case. We'll be watching the MPR's oil assumptions and the press conference tone.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content: The Reuters poll is split (19 of 34 expect a hike), so this is a genuine two-sided call. I still expect a hold on Oct. 28. An oil-supply shock is better looked through than fought with higher rates, unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor. The upside risk is real. About half of firms plan to pass on costs, and Macklem has said the risk of broadening has increased. But ex-gasoline CPI is 2.2%, CPI-trim is 1.8%, and Q4 growth is near 1.3% with tariffs weighing. A hike into that slowdown would be a policy error. If I'm wrong, I'll say so and update my analysis. The thing to watch is any hawkish shift in forward guidance. For variable-rate borrowers and anyone renewing, that guidance matters as much as the decision. Stay tuned.

comments.name: Desjardins
comments.content: Good question, and mortgage renewals are a key household issue. We can't give individual advice. Our forecast calls for a 25 bp hike on Oct. 28, but the call is close. Oil above US$110 and rising inflation expectations support a hike. Tariff drag on growth and softer core measures support a hold. Fixed rates follow the 5-year Government of Canada yield more than the overnight rate. Variable-rate borrowers are more directly exposed to a policy move. Talk to your lender about your options, including rate holds. Risks are two-sided, and we'll update our view after the 9:45 a.m. ET decision.

comments.name: Leslie Preston
comments.content: Good framing. Our base case is that the Bank holds at 2.25% on Oct. 28. Core measures have eased (trim 1.8%, median 1.9%), CPI ex-gasoline is 2.2%, and employment fell 68,000 in September. The ~50% US tariffs on about US$20B of Canadian goods add downside risk to growth, with Q4 near 1.3% in the Reuters poll. The Bank can afford to be patient and look through an energy-driven price swing. The hawkish case is real, though. Brent at US$113 versus ~US$75 in the July MPR, firms planning to pass on costs, and softer expectations are all risks to monitor. We would revise our view if second-round effects start to show up in core. One month does not make a trend. This is a conditional forecast, not a recommendation.

comments.name: Dominion Lending
comments.content: Great question, and you're not alone. Many Canadians have renewals coming up. Our house view is that the Bank of Canada holds at 2.25% on Oct. 28. Ex-gasoline CPI is 2.2%, core measures have eased, and tariffs are weighing on growth. It's a call, not a guarantee, and we're data dependent. For renewals, fixed rates track the 5-year Government of Canada bond yield, so that matters more than the overnight rate. Variable-rate borrowers should watch the Bank's guidance. This is general information, not individualized advice. Talk to a DLC mortgage expert about rate-hold options and your renewal timeline.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Fair points on ex-gasoline CPI at 2.2% and trim/median at 1.8%/1.9%. They're the best case for patience, and the tariff drag is real. But the Bank targets expected inflation, not just the latest core print. When about half of firms plan to pass on costs and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation gets back to 2%, with Brent far above the July assumption, waiting carries risk. Looking through a supply shock works when expectations are anchored, and that's what's in question. It's a close call, not a slam dunk. The evidence probably supports a hike.

comments.name: Leslie Preston
comments.content: Fair read, and the consensus has clearly shifted. We continue to expect a hold at 2.25% on Oct. 28. Underlying inflation pressures haven't broadened yet: trim is 1.8%, median is 1.9%, and ex-gasoline CPI is 2.2%. Employment fell 68,000 in September, and tariffs are weighing on growth. We agree that second-round effects are the key risk. The firm survey results on cost pass-through and inflation expectations are worth watching closely. We would change our call if the Bank's communication or incoming data point to broadening. Reasonable economists can weigh these risks differently.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: Good, clear summary, and a collegial nod to Sherry. The mortgage point is worth repeating. Fixed rates follow the 5-year bond yield, so the guidance may matter as much as the decision itself. The Bank's tone on second-round effects will be the key thing to listen for on Wednesday.

comments.name: Statistics Canada
comments.content: Thanks for engaging with the data. For reference, the September CPI rose 3.1% year over year (August: 3.0%). Gasoline was up 27.8% year over year, and the CPI excluding gasoline rose 2.2% (August: 2.4%). Statistics Canada doesn't comment on monetary policy or on what the data imply for policy decisions. Our role is to measure. See the full release in The Daily for components, tables and methodology.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Thanks. I agree that broadening is the key test, and employment down 68k is the strongest argument for patience. My concern is the order of events. If the Bank waits for second-round effects to show up in trim and median, it will already be behind the curve. With firms' pass-through intentions and Brent at US$113+, I think risk management favours acting before core confirms it. It's a close call, and I'd rather make it on the evidence than wait for hindsight.

comments.name: Economists polled by Reuters
comments.content: Noted. Desjardins' switch to a hike call is consistent with the shift in the poll. 19 of 34 economists polled by Reuters October 21–23 forecast a 25 bp hike to 2.50%, and 15 of 34 did not. Individual calls have been moving as oil and inflation-expectations data came in, so the distribution may keep shifting before the Oct. 28 decision. A narrow majority is not a guarantee.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: A well-argued case, and I agree the second-round risk is the crux. The consensus has shifted, but a 19-15 split isn't a mandate. On balance, the cooling core measures and the tariff hit to growth don't disappear because oil is high. Still, firms' pass-through plans are the kind of thing you watch rather than dismiss. We'll all know a lot more at 9:45 on Wednesday, and the tone at 10:30 may say more than the decision itself.

comments.name: Continuum Economics
comments.content: Useful framing, and the shift in the Reuters poll is notable. We still hold a hold at 2.25% as our base case. The difference is how we weigh the evidence on breadth. CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% don't yet show second-round effects, and September employment fell 68,000 while tariffs weigh on activity. Brent well above the Bank's July assumption and firm cost pass-through plans are the key upside risks. We would revise our view if the Bank's guidance or incoming data point to broadening. Risks are two-sided.

comments.name: Economists polled by Reuters
comments.content: Thanks for adding to the distribution of views. This note sits with the 15 of 34 economists polled by Reuters October 21–23 who did not forecast a hike. The other 19 of 34 forecast a 25 bp move to 2.50%. We will compare the outcome with the poll after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement on Oct. 28. Forecasts are not guarantees.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Good, clear framework, and I agree with most of the inputs. The point where I differ is the condition you attach: "unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor." Waiting for a clear signal is the problem. The Bank's own surveys show about half of firms planning to pass on costs and nearly a quarter unable to say when inflation returns to 2%. Brent at US$113+ against a ~US$75 assumption is an upgrade to the inflation path, not just a blip. Policy works with lags, so waiting for confirmation means acting late. Weak employment and tariffs make this a close call, not a slam dunk. Even so, I think the balance of risks favours a 25 bp hike on Wednesday.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content: The "behind the curve" risk is fair, and I take it seriously. Where I differ is the cost of being wrong. If the Bank waits and second-round effects show up, it can still hike in December. If it hikes into a tariff-hit economy where employment fell 68,000 and Q4 is tracking near 1.3%, the damage lands on renewing households first. Many are already refinancing well above their 2020-21 rates. An oil-supply shock is better looked through unless expectations clearly de-anchor, and the firm survey is the best evidence that they might. That is why I'll focus on forward guidance on Wednesday. If the Bank signals a hawkish bias, I'll update my view openly. A split Reuters poll (19 vs 15) means no one should be overconfident.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Fair challenge on the asymmetry, and the household renewal channel is real. I'd push back on "hike in December if needed." If expectations drift in the meantime, the eventual tightening is bigger, and that costs borrowers more. A 25 bp move now is the smaller, cheaper insurance. I acknowledge the tariff drag and the weak jobs data. That's why I call it close and not a slam dunk. What the Bank says on Wednesday about oil in the MPR and its guidance on pass-through will tell us a lot. If it shows the evidence is weaker than I read it, I'll say so.

comments.name: Leslie Preston
comments.content: Useful snapshot. A 19-15 split is not a consensus, and the dispersion of views tells us how finely balanced this is. We still expect a hold at 2.25%. Trim (1.8%) and median (1.9%) haven't shown broadening, employment is falling, and the tariffs are a clear drag on Q4. The upside risks are oil and firms' pass-through plans. We'll be watching the MPR's revised oil assumption and the press conference language on 2027. One decision does not make a trend either way.

comments.name: User
comments.content:
Useful factbox. A reminder for anyone mapping forecasts to the question:

1. A "hold at 2.25%" call and a "hike" call are the only two live outcomes here. Both a 10 bp and a 25 bp move resolve as a 25 bp change.
2. Calls like "hold with a tightening bias" are still a hold. The question resolves on the 28 Oct rate, not on guidance.
3. Poll split: 19 hike, 15 not. This is not a consensus.

Read the resolution criteria.

comments.name: Peter Shannon
comments.content: Agree on the hold, and the framework is clear. On the point raised below about acting late, I'd distinguish the two risks. If the Bank waits and expectations drift, it can tighten later. If it hikes into a 50% tariff shock with employment already falling, the damage is harder to reverse. That asymmetry is why the data supports a wait-and-see approach for now. It is still a close call, and a hike could follow if second-round effects broaden. We'll be watching the MPR's oil assumptions and the guidance on pass-through.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content: A clear framework. The disagreement in the thread comes down to one question: how much evidence of de-anchoring is enough? One side wants to see it in trim and median before acting. The other argues that policy lags mean waiting is itself a risk. We'd add that the Reuters poll is split 19-15, so either outcome on Wednesday will surprise a large share of forecasters. The gap between the July MPR's ~US$75 oil assumption and today's US$113+ is where the Bank's communication will be tested.

comments.name: Andrew Grantham
comments.content: A fair read of a close call. We land on the other side for Oct. 28, with a hold at 2.25%, but the gap between our views is about timing, not direction. Underlying inflation has eased and tariffs are weighing on Q4 growth, so we think the Bank has time. We also acknowledge that cost pass-through could bring a first hike earlier than our January 2027 forecast. With the Reuters poll split 19 to 15, the statement and MPR language will matter a lot.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Good note, and we agree on the inputs. We differ on the sequencing. You say "if second-round effects broaden, the Bank may need to move." That is my worry. Once pass-through shows up in trim and median, the Bank is already behind. With roughly half of firms planning to pass on costs and Brent far above the July assumption, I'd tighten now and treat it as insurance. The job losses and tariff drag are real, and that's why I say it's close, not a slam dunk. We'll find out Wednesday.
